Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Israel Israel facing water shortages caused by destruction of Gaza’s treatment plants Five desalination plants shut down for days, while Gaza remains in grip of severe water and sanitation crisis Lorenzo Tondo in Jerualem and Seham Tantesh in Gaza Thu 24 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom crippled much of its desalination capacity, in a crisis scientists say was triggered when Israeli attacks destroyed much of Gaza’s wastewater infrastructure, causing a massive discharge of untreated sewage. “Pollution does not recognise political borders,” said the Zalul Environmental Association, an Israeli NGO dedicated to protecting the country’s seas and shores. “The discharge of untreated sewage from the Gaza Strip into the sea is contributing to the worsening crisis affecting the Israeli desalination facilities. The wastewater contains nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed microalgae and cyanobacteria and may intensify their blooms.” Despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, Gaza remains gripped by a severe water and sanitation crisis . The Palestinian territory is plagued by rodents, and sewage floods its coastline after Israel destroyed its wastewater treatment plants. Just across the border, a vast bloom of microalgae stretching up to 60 miles (100km) long has clogged filters at five of Israel’s six main desalination plants, which were shut down for days and have since been operating at a reduced level. View image in fullscreen A satellite view shows an algae bloom along Gaza’s coast to Ashdod in Israel. Photograph: Sentinal Hub/Copernicus.eu Experts say that after nearly three years of war, the environmental consequences of the destruction in Gaza are now spilling back into Israel. “The discharge of untreated sewage from Gaza into the sea increases risks to Israel’s water production infrastructure along the southern Mediterranean coast,” said Jack Gilron, a professor emeritus and desalination expert at Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research. “The current incident reinforces the need to prepare against threats to one of Israel’s main sources of drinking water.” Since 7 October 2023, Israeli bombardment has destroyed 90% of Gaza’s water and sanitation infrastructure, according to a report by Médecins Sans Frontières . Direct strikes have been carried out on wells, carrier lines, reservoirs and desalination units. Gaza’s water crisis remains severe. Before the war, 80% the territory’s supply came from an aquifer under the coastal strip, but that supply is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater and unfit for human consumption. Most of Gaza’s drinking water came from desalination plants and three pipelines controlled by the Israeli water authority, but those pipelines were cut at the start of the war and have only partially reopened . View image in fullscreen In Gaza City, a reservoir has become a sewage collection pool after the destruction of local wastewater infrastructure and pumping stations. Photograph: Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images Meanwhile, damaged or destroyed distribution networks have left much of the population reliant on water trucks. For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease, with acute diarrhoea among the leading causes of illness. “We carry water in jerry cans,” said Nas al-Barawi, 34, a mother of five from Beit Lahia. “We walk with heavy containers or wait for hours in queues. Much of the water is unsafe, and children suffer recurring stomach infections, diarrhoea and skin rashes. Damaged sewage networks and failed pumps have also left wastewater flowing between tents and through residential areas.” Omar Shatat, the deputy executive director of the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility in Gaza, said all five of the territory’s wastewater treatment plants were out of service, leaving an estimated 45,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage to flow into the Mediterranean every day. In addition, about 15,000 cubic metres of untreated waste a day seeps into the groundwater from soakaway pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi. “This is a catastrophic situation environmentally and from a public-health perspective,” Shatat said. “The sea is heavily polluted, and the first people affected are Gaza’s residents and displaced people because they are in direct contact with the highest concentrations of sewage.” View image in fullscreen A man crosses effluent water that runs from the camps housing displaced families in Gaza City towards the Mediterranean. Photograph: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP/Getty Images Pat Griffiths, the International Committee of the Red Cross’s spokesperson in Gaza City, said the situation was only likely to get worse with the onset of winter. “Palestinians live surrounded by wastewater. It’s all around them. It’s where they eat, where they get water, where they walk,” he said. Shaimaa al-Katari, 37, who has been displaced to al-Mawasi, said: “We have nowhere to dispose of the water from washing dishes and clothes. We have to let it run into the street, which causes pools of stagnant water to form. Algae and mosquitoes then spread around them and the streets become dirty. We suffer from foul smells, mosquitoes at night and flies during the day, as well as rodents.” Rats have infested parts of Gaza for months, thriving amid raw sewage and piles of rubbish accumulating around overcrowded camps for displaced people. View image in fullscreen The Bureij refugee camp in Gaza is fumigated against rodents and insects as infectious diseases increase. Photograph: Hassan Jedi/Anadolu/Getty Images Israeli communities near the Gaza border have also been grappling with an unprecedented rat infestation , with rodents swarming homes and gardens. “The consequences [of the war] do not stop at the border,” said Nada Majdalani, the Palestine director of EcoPeace Middle East, an environmental peacebuilding organisation. “We are already seeing an increase in hepatitis A in Gaza. I believe we are on the verge of a catastrophe. And a serious outbreak in Gaza would not necessarily remain within Gaza’s borders.” In Israel, authorities are urging people to use water “judiciously” until the system is fully restored. Water supplies have been reduced in the south of the country, and farmers have been instructed to halt irrigation, which economists say will cause food prices to rise. Zalul and EcoPeace urged Cogat, the Israeli agency charged with administration of Gaza, to help restore the territory’s sewage system and allow wastewater to be treated in Israeli-controlled areas. Cogat did not respond to a request for comment. Zalul said: “If the pollution continues, its impact could eventually be felt throughout the country. When the marine environment is contaminated, both people and nature suffer. Regardless of which side of the border they are on.” How Israel created a water crisis for Palestinians – video Explore more on these topics Israel Gaza Palestine Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.baltictimes.com/airbaltic_no.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive airBaltic no longer focusing on size of its route network, but rather on its depth - Martinovs 2026-09-10 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Latvia's national airline airBaltic is no longer focusing on the size of its route network, but rather on its depth, said Andrejs Martinovs, chairman of the airBaltic board, in an interview with LETA. He noted that, in accordance with the shareholders’ letter of expectations, airBaltic will continue to ensure connectivity and maintain Riga as a transportation hub for the Baltic states. "What may change is that we will delve deeper into analyzing demand. If a route has fewer leisure travelers but sufficient interest from business passengers, airBaltic may even increase the number of flights. The main change is that we are no longer focusing on the size of the route network, but rather on its depth," Martinovs emphasized. He explained that if there is visible demand for several routes - not only from leisure travelers but also from business travelers - then airBaltic assumes there is also an economic benefit underlying that demand. Thus, Martinovs believes that, overall, the new business plan will not harm connectivity, leisure travelers, or business traffic. "We simply will not boast as much in the future about airBaltic flying to some exotic destination or that the number of destinations has increased by such-and-such a percent. Instead, let us increase the number of flights on a truly busy route and give those same business travelers the opportunity to fly there in the morning and be back by evening," explained Martinovs. LETA previously reported that airBaltic will offer 59 direct routes from Riga during the 2027 summer season, which is approximately 20 percent fewer than during this year’s summer season. However, two destinations - Madeira and Sharm el-Sheikh - to which airBaltic will operate flights during the upcoming winter season, will be included in the route network for only one month, April, during the next summer season; after that, the route network will consist of 57 destinations. During the upcoming summer season, flights will no longer be operated to Aberdeen, Scotland; Antalya, Turkey; Batumi, Georgia; Bergen, Norway; Dublin, Ireland; Yerevan, Armenia; Faro, Portugal; Gothenburg, Sweden; Malta; Olbia, Italy; and Valencia, Spain. Flights to Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, however, are scheduled for the winter season. The airline emphasized that, although the number of routes is technically smaller, the number of seats offered is equivalent to that of the 2026 summer season. https://www.runcornandwidnesworld.co.uk/.text: Court Thief 'deliberately targeted' woman in Widnes carpet shop By Magen Kelly Reporter Share 0 Comments 2 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A thief 'deliberately targeted' a woman in Widnes town centre, stealing £1,200 from her handbag as she visited a carpet shop. Marian Vasile, 53, who currently lives in Wythenshawe but is originally from Romania, pleaded guilty on August 6, and attended Warrington Magistrates Court on Wednesday September 9, for sentencing. The court heard how Mr Vasile, along with three others, stole £1,200 from the victim, whilst she was in Treadwell Carpets in Widnes. The defendant, along with the others, followed the woman from Santander Bank where she withdrew the money, to Treadwell Carpets. Once in the shop, the defendant distracted the manager, who was in conversation with the woman, while other members of the group distracted the victim and stole the money from her bag. Cheshire Police (Image: Newsquest) Prosecution for the case said that the woman had been 'deliberately targeted', and that planning had gone into the theft. Mr Vasile did not have any representation but was accompanied by an interpreter. When asked if he had anything to say to the magistrates, he replied: “I regret what I have done and I am very sorry for what happened.” The magistrates granted Mr Vasile an 18-month custodial sentence due to previous convictions, which was then reduced to 12-months because of his guilty plea. This was suspended for 12-months. The defendant was also required to pay £300 compensation to the victim, one quarter of the £1,200 stolen by the group. Due to the defendant’s financial situation, no court costs or surcharges were applied to the fine, to ensure that the victim received her full compensation. It was agreed that the defendant’s wife would pay £50 per month to settle the fine. A Home Office Spokesperson said: "Any foreign national who receives a prison sentence in the UK is referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity and will be barred from ever returning. “Over 11,700 foreign criminals have been removed since the last election.” Court Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/2.text: WEEKEND WALK Weekend Walk Leisure Walking and outdoors Walk Buckden Pike and visit the Polish War Memorial Weekend Walk Leisure Walking and outdoors By Jonathan Smith Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The head of Wharfedale is surrounded by four of the Dales 30 Mountains (all over 2,000ft high). The one to the east is Buckden Pike, the most enjoyable of the four. Add in the Polish War Memorial on the summit ridge for an excellent day out. I always enjoy getting the main climbing out of the way early, so exit the car park via a gate at its north end and head on a wide track to the steep flanks of Buckden Pike, initially skirting the steepest ground. After passing through some pleasant woodland the track turns north east and, after a further 200 metres, divides at a small gate. A signpost points uphill to Buckden Pike. From here the path climbs steadily just north of east for one mile until it meets a wall near some steeper ground. Follow the wall (on your left) south east up some rock steps to the summit of Buckden Pike. Looking up Buckden Beck (Image: Jonathan Smith) The summit is distinctive; a trig point and a large cairn with a neighbouring, even taller post next to it. The views are superb in all directions, particularly to the west where all of the better known Yorkshire Three Peaks are displayed, and to the north towards the Howgills and the mountains above the valley of Mallerstang. Buckden Pike walk map (Image: Jonathan Smith) Buckden Pike is one of the ‘Dales 30’ mountains; a challenge describing every mountain in the Yorkshire Dales over 2,000 feet. It is a satisfying and achievable challenge and to complete all 30 will bring you to wonderful, rarely visited areas such as this. Head south along the wide summit ridge for nearly a mile, next to a wall and with a pleasant surprise at its conclusion. Just where the ridge starts to drop away look over the wall for the Polish War Memorial. The cross is dedicated to the six Polish air crew who crashed on Buckden Pike in 1942 on a training exercise in bad winter weather. There was only one survivor, Jo, who was able to crawl to the pub at Cray and later helped commission the memorial. Look closely at the base of the cross - parts of the aircraft are embedded in it. Buckden Pike cross (Image: Jonathan Smith) It is possible to carry on south and join a bridleway which winds its way gradually down towards Starbotton, but I prefer returning towards the summit and taking a faint permissive path heading west at the stone wall, just to the south of the summit trig. This leads south west down some steep slopes before arriving at the top of Buckden Gill and the remains of a 19th Century lead mine. Do not be tempted to head down the gill but cross the little wooden bridge and take the footpath above the stone wall heading just west of south for three quarters of a mile. Follow the wall to the point it turns steeply downhill. A short cut directly down to the village is possible but it is more sensible to carry on south for a further one third of a mile to a further wall junction and a more obvious path. The path then drops and reverses itself as it heads north back towards the car park at Buckden. Walk facts Distance: Roughly six miles. Height to climb: 500m (1,640 feet). Start: SD 942774. There is a large car park at the north end of Buckden. The toilets were open with suitable hygiene last week. Difficulty: Medium/hard. A steep climb in places is followed by a descent on intermittent paths. Some of the going is quite rough. Refreshments: The Buck Inn in Buckden is the most popular place for a drink or snack. Be prepared: The route description and sketch map only provide a guide to the walk. You must take out and be able to read a map (O/S Explorer OL30) and in cloudy/misty conditions a compass. You must also wear the correct clothing and footwear for the outdoors. Whilst every effort is made to provide accurate information, walkers head out at their own risk. Please observe the Countryside Code and park sensibly. Jonathan Smith runs Where2walk, a walking company based in the Yorkshire Dales. He has written four books on walking in the Dales, The Yorkshire 3 Peaks, Walks without Stiles, The Dales 30 mountains a guide to The Bracken Way. Visit Where2walk where you can buy the books. Jonathan runs navigation training courses for all levels. The next beginner/refresher course is at Long Preston on September 26. You can buy Dales 30 guide books, t-shirts and caps from the new Dales 30 website. Start the challenge today. Where2walk.co.uk features hundreds of walks with descriptions across Yorkshire and beyond, from easy strolls to harder climbs. Visit the website for details of all these walks, guiding days and navigation course.
